original_value: This paper presents a systematic analysis of a game controlled by a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) based on Steady-State Visually Evoked Potentials (SSVEP). The objective is to understand BCI systems from the Human-Computer Interface (HCI) point of view, by observing how the users interact with the game and evaluating how the interface elements influence the system performance. The interactions of 30 volunteers with our computer game, named “Get Coins,” through a BCI based on SSVEP, have generated a database of brain signals and the corresponding responses to a questionnaire about various perceptual parameters, such as visual stimulation, acoustic feedback, background music, visual contrast, and visual fatigue. Each one of the volunteers played one match using the keyboard and four matches using the BCI, for comparison. In all matches using the BCI, the volunteers achieved the goals of the game. Eight of them achieved a perfect score in at least one of the four matches, showing the feasibility of the direct communication between the brain and the computer. Despite this successful experiment, adaptations and improvements should be implemented to make this innovative technology accessible to the end user.

result.paraphrase: This paper offers a systematic study of a game controlled through a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) based on Steady-State Visually Evoked Potentials (SSVEP). Its aim is to understand BCI systems from a Human-Computer Interface (HCI) perspective by examining user interaction with the game and assessing how interface elements affect system performance. Thirty volunteers played our computer game, Get Coins, via an SSVEP-based BCI, producing a database of brain signals along with questionnaire responses on perceptual factors including visual stimulation, acoustic feedback, background music, visual contrast, and visual fatigue. For comparison, each volunteer played one match with the keyboard and four matches using the BCI. In every BCI match, the volunteers met the game objectives. Eight achieved a perfect score in at least one of the four matches, demonstrating the feasibility of direct communication between the brain and the computer. Even so, adaptations and improvements are still needed to make this innovative technology accessible to end users.
